instruction.text: You will hear a radio interview with Luis Martinez, a professor of social sciences who conducts research on the concept of generations and its connection to economic developments. While listening, tick the correct answer. There is only one correct answer.

atoms.sound: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>Good evening, my name is Troy Kopernick, and you’re listening to Science Lines, live. Today we’re talking about intergenerational fairness—and we’ll start with something very concrete: unequal starting chances at labour-market entry. A recent meta-analysis on ‘unemployment scarring’ pulls together a large body of research and finds that an early spell of unemployment often leaves long shadows—especially in later wages. We now have Professor Martinez from Atkinson University on the line. Professor Martinez, you’re a social scientist who studies life-course inequality. Why do these early shocks matter so much?</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>Good afternoon Troy, thanks for having me! Because the timing isn’t random across birth cohorts. If you finish school or training during a recession, you face a systematically different opportunity structure than someone who graduates in a boom. The evidence suggests that bad initial conditions can push people into jobs below their skill level, weaker employers, or unstable contracts—and those first placements shape the next steps.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>So the ‘starting line’ is already skewed?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>Exactly. Think of it as cumulative advantage, just in reverse. In many studies on graduating in a recession, earnings losses persist for years—often close to a decade. The mechanism is not only lower wages at the start, but slower movement toward better-paying firms. It’s a mobility problem as much as a wage problem.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>And it’s not only about pay, right? People often say: ‘You’ll catch up eventually.’</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>Some catch up; some don’t. And even where incomes recover, there can be other scars. Research links unemployment and weak early careers to poorer health outcomes. There’s also work suggesting that graduating in an economic downturn can raise risks of mental health problems. At the same time, we should be careful: a minority of studies even find a “bright side” in attitudes—some recession entrants report higher job satisfaction later, possibly because expectations recalibrate. So the honest summary is: the dominant pattern is economic and health risk, but the subjective experience can be complex.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>That brings us to the bigger question: is it even helpful to speak of “generations” here—Gen Z, Millennials, and so on?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>It can be helpful, but it’s also methodologically dangerous. Many apparent 'generation effects' are really age effects or period effects in disguise. The core challenge is separating what changes because people get older, what changes because the historical moment changes, and what changes because cohorts differ. In addition, even within a cohort, it cannot simply be assumed that everyone has the same starting opportunities – this depends heavily on the financial, cultural and social capital of the parents.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>Yet people do feel like they belong to a generation.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>Yes—because generational identity is socially produced. Shared formative events become public narratives: in media, in politics, in workplaces, and in families. Over time, those stories solidify into boundaries: ‘we had it harder,’ or ‘they had it easier.’ Those comparisons can mobilise solidarity—but also resentment.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>If we bring it back to fairness: what would a ‘generation-just’ response look like?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m1Us_chirp'>It would treat recessions as collective risks that shouldn’t permanently penalise the unlucky cohorts who happen to enter the labour market at the wrong moment. Practically, that means automatic stabilisers for young entrants—stronger training and re-training, targeted hiring incentives, and reliable income protection that prevents early setbacks from becoming lifelong disadvantages.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m6Us_chirp'>Professor Martinez, thank you for joining us live.</voice>
